description: 6 Innovators. 1 Mission. Fusing teamwork and bold vision to solve the next big space challenge.
summary:
Etna is a web dashboard, powered by super intelligence (SI), that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire-safety answers for crewed habitats. NASA PSI holds 24 combustion investigations: 2,128 test rows and 67 reports spread across spreadsheets and PDFs. We cleaned all of it and linked every number to its source table row or report page.

Users pick where their crew will live: the ISS, a Moon habitat, a pressurized rover or a Mars habitat. Etna then ranks the investigations by how many tests were actually measured in that habitat's oxygen and pressure, and groups findings by prevention, detection and suppression. A coverage map shows the critical gap: only 20 tests fall inside planned Moon-habitat air (at least 30% O2, 10.2 psi or less), and none were run in lunar gravity.

An SI assistant answers questions only from report passages and test tables, and it cites them. It also says plainly when NASA has no data. Etna adds NASA's own acrylic flammability boundary (BASS-II), a 3D fuel-droplet Flame Lab built on the nearest real tests and models scored on held-out test days, a knowledge graph and CSV export for modelers. Three explanation levels serve everyone from students to researchers.

As crews return to the Moon in more oxygen-rich air, Etna shows what we know about fire and where we have not looked.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA has burned thousands of flames in microgravity, and its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository makes the results public. But they are spread over 24 investigations, dozens of spreadsheets and more than 2,300 report pages. They are hard to find, harder to compare and harder still to interpret. The stakes are rising: to shorten spacesuit pre-breathing, Moon habitats and pressurized rovers are expected to run at 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less. That is over 40% more oxygen than Earth's air, and materials become much more flammable. Designers need to know what NASA actually measured in that air, and what it never tested.

WHAT ETNA DOES

Etna answers one question: "What do we really know about fire in the air my crew will breathe?" Every answer points back to the exact NASA test row or report page.

1. Home, "Where will your crew live?": choose the ISS, a Moon habitat, a pressurized rover or a Mars habitat. All 24 investigations are ranked by how many of their tests were measured inside that habitat's oxygen and pressure range. Badges read "in this air", "just outside it (near-lunar)" or "no tests in this air". Hovering a card highlights its tests on a mini coverage map. Four Earth-facing evidence cards (smoke detectors, extinguishers, materials, ventilation) each link to their NASA source.

2. Experiments: every investigation as a card, filtered by fuel family (solid materials, liquid droplets, gas flames, smoke and dust, ground studies) and by fire-safety job (prevention, detection, suppression).

3. Study details: summary, objectives, sourced findings (each linked to its report page), why the study matters for fire safety, a link to the NASA PSI page, and "Download test data (CSV)" with the cleaned, unit-normalized rows, ready for predictive modeling. Each study also has its own SI chat, limited to that study's card, reports and tests.

4. Coverage map: every test with oxygen and pressure, plotted against the ISS and Moon-habitat/rover air zones, with a dashed near-lunar band. Hover a dot to see its study, fuel and source row. It makes the gap visible: only 20 tests (all gas flames from one ACME experiment) sit inside planned Moon-habitat air. Seventeen FLEX droplet tests are about 1 kPa outside, and none of those flames went out on its own.

5. Knowledge graph: experiments, materials, fuel families, habitats, safety jobs and hardware (CIR with ACME, CIR with MDCA, MSG, Cygnus/Saffire) shown as a connected network, filterable by habitat and node type. It lets users compare investigations by shared fuels, hardware and conditions.

6. Predict: will an acrylic (PMMA) rod keep burning? The app uses NASA's own flammability boundary from the BASS-II report (Eq. 6.1). Pick the rod size, oxygen and airflow, and see which side of the curve you are on, against ISS and Moon-habitat reference levels.

7. Flame Lab: a 3D burning fuel droplet (FLEX and CFI fuels). Choose a habitat or custom air, fuel, O2, pressure, droplet size and diluent (CO2, He, N2). The droplet shrinks and goes out the way the five nearest real NASA tests did, including the near-invisible cool flame, and a size-over-time chart is drawn. Trained models give a second opinion with a trust badge: "tested here", "between tests" or "outside tested range".

8. Ask Etna, the SI assistant: a chat panel on every page. It searches the reports, reads the study cards, queries the test tables, draws charts and cites every claim. When NASA has no data, it says so.

9. Report search (Ctrl+K): searches every NASA report page in your own words. It merges full-text and semantic (BGE-M3 embedding) search, and each result shows its report and page.

10. My reports: upload your own PDF. It is indexed, gets its own chat and receives an SI-drafted study card (summary, findings, limitations). A person reviews, edits, approves or rejects the card. Only approved cards join the collection, and they are always labelled as uploads, never as NASA data.

11. Fire stories, interactive history: the 1997 Mir oxygen-generator fire and the 2006 ISS Elektron leak. Users make the crew's decisions. Choices that match the record follow what happened, and other branches are clearly labelled "imagined". A debrief cites NASA and ESA sources.

12. "Did you know?": short curated facts from NASA experiment findings and NASA Spinoff (for example, the fine-water-mist extinguisher), each linked to its source. These show Earth applications of the research.

13. Three explanation levels: Explorer (plain language, with an "Explain it simply" guided tour), Student (exact numbers) and Researcher (full detail). Each level changes both the text and the assistant's persona. The app has light and dark modes and works on phones.

HOW IT WORKS, AND WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT

- Data pipeline: a downloader pulls all 24 PSI combustion investigations. Each test table is cleaned into CSV with units normalized and every change logged. We re-checked every claim against the raw files and PDFs (VERIFICATION.md in the repo).

- Hand extraction: the outcomes of about 250 BASS and BASS-II solid-material tests existed only as tables inside PDF reports. We transcribed them with a page reference and a confidence note on every row.

- Strict habitat rules: a test counts for a habitat only if both its chamber O2 and its pressure fall inside the habitat's range. Near-lunar tests are shown separately and never counted as lunar. Oxygen blown from a burner (CFI-G) is never treated as cabin air.

- Predictors: small, readable logistic and ridge regression models, each scored on whole test days it never saw. For example, the droplet early-extinction model reaches 81% accuracy against a 68% baseline (AUC 0.85), and the cool-flame outcome model reaches 79% against 59% (AUC 0.87). Gradient boosting was tried and never clearly won, so we kept the simpler models. Solid materials have no model on purpose, because the data is too thin.

- The SI writes the words, never the numbers: counts, rankings, the coverage map, the PMMA boundary and all predictions are computed directly from NASA data.

- Three boundaries are shown throughout the app: air is not gravity (all evidence is microgravity), near is not in range, and an estimate is not a measurement. Partial gravity is shown as a gap, not predicted.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Engineers and mission planners see at once which evidence applies to a given habitat atmosphere, and where new tests (for example LUCI or FM2 in lunar gravity) are most needed.

- Researchers and students get clean, sourced, downloadable data and a REST API for their own flammability models.

- Educators and the public get an accessible, honest entry point to space fire safety and its Earth spinoffs.

- The upload-and-review workflow lets the collection grow as new reports (including future partial-gravity data) are published.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Frontend: React 18, Vite, Three.js (Flame Lab 3D), d3-force/d3-zoom (knowledge graph), Mermaid (assistant diagrams); custom SVG charts and characters.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL on Neon with pgvector.

- SI: gpt-oss-120b served by Groq through the Agno agent framework (assistant, study chats, draft study cards); BGE-M3 embeddings through sentence-transformers and PyTorch (semantic report search); scikit-learn-style logistic and ridge models exported to JSON and run with the standard library.

- Data processing: Python standard library and pypdf for PSI download, cleaning, PDF text extraction and training.

- Deployment: Docker on Google Cloud Run, with Firebase Hosting at etna.web.app.

WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

- It is habitat-first rather than database-first: users start from where people will live, not from experiment acronyms.

- It is honest by design: trust badges, near-lunar bands and labelled illustrations show the limits of the evidence instead of hiding them.

- One dataset serves three audiences through three explanation levels, each with its own guide.

- Interactive history (Mir 1997 and ISS 2006) gives the data an emotional reason to matter.

- Users can bring their own reports, with a human approving every SI-drafted card.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (no extrapolation to Moon or Mars gravity), traceability of every number, the challenge's prevention/detection/suppression framing, the planned lunar atmosphere (30% O2 or more, 10.2 psi or less), accessibility for non-experts, mobile use, and keeping SI-generated content clearly separate from NASA data.

Live app: https://etna.web.app

Source code: https://github.com/Abderrahmane-Najib/Flame-in-Freefall
